<reflection>
The first experiment (S=2.0, cat=0.05, P=0.2) resulted in very similar negative log-likelihoods for almost all models (around -24 to -23), with the exception of M20. This indicates that under standard catalytic conditions (low catalyst mol%, moderate substrate), the models are highly flexible and can adjust their rate constants to fit the data equally well. My aim to broadly separate the mechanisms was only partially achieved, as the chosen regime did not sufficiently penalize incorrect structural assumptions (e.g., higher-order catalyst dependencies or specific deactivation pathways). We need to probe a regime where the structural differences in the rate laws become dominant.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To break the degeneracy between the models, we must move away from the standard pseudo-steady-state regime. I propose an experiment with the maximum allowed catalyst concentration ([cat]0 = 0.20) and a low substrate concentration ([S]0 = 0.5), with no initial product ([P]0 = 0.0). 
1. The high catalyst loading (40 mol%) will drastically amplify second-order catalyst interactions, strongly differentiating mechanisms involving `2cat` (M2, M3, M13) or `cat + catS` (M5, M19) from standard first-order catalyst mechanisms.
2. The near-equimolar ratio of catalyst to substrate will violate the steady-state approximation. A significant fraction of the substrate will be rapidly bound in the transient phase, making the kinetics highly sensitive to the exact binding stoichiometry and the distribution between free `cat` and `catS`.
3. Starting with [P]0 = 0.0 provides a clean baseline to contrast with Run 1, helping to isolate product-induced deactivation (M12, M17) when analyzed jointly with the first dataset.
</hypothesis>
